items.abstract: Structured generation underpins large language model (LLM) agents that produce JSON, SQL, and function calls, where a single wrong field can cause the downstream action to fail. Constrained decoding already tracks parser transitions to enforce formal validity, and these transitions expose how generated tokens participate in schema-critical decisions such as required fields, arguments, and structural boundaries under the active grammar. PASK addresses the mismatch between model-side KV sensitivity and task-level structured risk by using task-error sensitivity to set minimum protection floors and attention-output distortion to allocate residual KV capacity. items.title: RECAST: Recent & Context-Aware Sampling for Test-Time Adaptation in Streaming Biosignals
items.abstract: Streaming biosignals vary across subjects and drift over time, so population-trained models lose accuracy during long-term monitoring. Test-time adaptation (TTA) enables online personalization by updating the model on incoming samples. But in a stream, a basic question is left open: \emph{which samples should drive each update?} Using all buffered samples blurs the update with irrelevant segments. Using only the latest segment makes the update noisy and unstable. The most useful samples are recent, aligned with the current physiological state, and reliable enough to learn from. We propose \textbf{RECAST} (REcent \& Context-Aware Sampling for TTA), a lightweight sampling module for buffered TTA frameworks. RECAST builds each adaptation batch from three signals: temporal recency, contextual similarity, and predictive reliability. It changes only which samples are used, leaving the model and the training objective unchanged. items.title: Spatial-Semantic Reasoning using Large Language Models for Efficient UAV Search Operations
items.abstract: We present a real-time semantic navigation framework for Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) focused on improving time efficiency in the Object Goal Navigation (ObjectNav) task. Central to our approach is a Large Language Model (LLM) that interprets user-provided natural language instructions and performs semantic reasoning over detected objects and spatial context to prioritize high-probability search regions. The system combines real-time object detection, 3D spatial mapping, and polynomial spline interpolation for smooth and feasible UAV trajectory planning. Unlike prior methods that rely on offline reasoning or simulator-constrained action spaces, our framework can operate in real time, continuously updating semantic relevance based on new observations. Experiments in both simulated and real-world settings demonstrate reductions in mission duration while maintaining high search accuracy, underscoring the effectiveness of LLM-guided reasoning for time- efficient UAV-based ObjectNav.

items.title: Finding Where the Buck Stops: An Automated Failure Attribution-Based Reflection Framework for Multi-Agent Collaboration
items.abstract: Multi-agent systems (MAS) powered by large language models have shown promise for complex tasks but suffer from high failure rates. items.title: Regime-Aware Portfolio Management via Retrieval-Augmented LLM-Guided Expert Switching
items.abstract: Financial markets are inherently non-stationary, making the effectiveness of individual portfolio-management strategies highly dependent on changing market conditions. This work proposes a retrieval-augmented expert-switching framework that dynamically selects portfolio management experts based on their historical performance under similar market situations. items.abstract: The rapid expansion of reusable skill repositories makes skill routing a critical capability for large language model (LLM) agents. items.title: Efficient Online Continual Foundation Model Fine-Tuning for Predictive Process Monitoring
items.abstract: Predictive Process Monitoring (PPM) models are increasingly deployed in dynamic environments where concept drift causes the underlying process distribution to shift over time. items.title: D-TAIA: Domain-Aware LLM Adaptation for Multi-Task Predictive Process Monitoring
items.abstract: Predictive Process Monitoring (PPM) enables organizations to forecast future process behavior, such as the next activity and remaining time of ongoing cases. In practice, three conditions cause existing methods to degrade, namely data scarcity, high process entropy and distributional shift. While Foundation Models (FMs), especially Large Language Models (LLMs), offer a new paradigm through broad sequential reasoning, adapting them to multi-task PPM under these conditions remains an open challenge. Existing FM-based approaches either lack mechanisms for handling distributional shift or rely on direct regression heads that can be structurally misaligned with continuous time prediction tasks. This paper introduces D-TAIA (Domain-aware Training and Attention-based Inference Architecture), a framework for a joint next activity and remaining time prediction task via parameter-efficient fine-tuning of an FM backbone. items.title: Stay Within Your Bounds: Distance-Guided Decoding for Guaranteed Context-Free Grammar Compliance
items.abstract: Grammar-constrained decoding helps large language models produce syntactically valid structured outputs, such as code, JSON, and SQL. For context-free grammars, many practical decoders enforce local prefix feasibility: each token must keep the current prefix extendable to some valid completion. Yet, under tokenizer-grammar mismatch and finite token budgets, feasible prefixes may still fail to reach acceptance. We propose a lookahead-guided decoding framework for context-free grammars based on pushdown automata. Offline, we compute bounded pushdown summaries with reachability labels and upper-bound distances to acceptance. Online, these estimates guide horizon-aware pruning and beam search. The resulting decoder is syntactically sound: every output is accepted by the target grammar. Experiments on JSON, SQL, and Linear Temporal Logic (LTL) show both consistent syntactic validity and improved completion quality over existing baselines.

items.title: Generative AI Alignment with Hinduism's Theological Plurality and Sacred Representation
items.abstract: Generative AI systems are increasingly used to answer personal questions and mediate everyday practices, including religion. items.title: Fine-Tuning Autobidders with Group Relative Policy Optimization
items.abstract: Automated bidding (autobidding) is a core component of modern online advertising systems. Within this component, advertisers delegate sequential bid decisions to algorithms that must maximize campaign value while adhering to constraints such as a limited budget and a target cost-per-click (CPC). One of the approaches to resolve the autobidding problem is to formulate it as a Markov decision process and use reinforcement learning (RL) to train a bid generation function. items.title: Performative Privacy: When Differential Privacy Maximizes Utility
items.abstract: Privacy-preserving learning is often motivated by the idea that protecting users' data can preserve trust and thus participation, improving utility in the long term. However, this claim has not been formalized so far. In parallel, performative learning provides a framework for studying learning systems whose deployment affects the data they later observe. In this work, we bring these two perspectives together and introduce \emph{performative privacy}, where data leakage reduces future participation. We study a simple model where agents repeatedly contribute data for mean estimation but may leave the system when their data is leaked. Privacy is implemented through differentially private mechanisms, creating a trade-off between estimation noise and future participation. We show, through a theoretical study of the dynamics and numerical experiments, that a finite privacy budget can outperform non-private estimation in the long term when the feedback loop between leakage and participation is sufficiently strong. This provides first evidence that differential privacy can be optimal not only as a protection mechanism, but also from the perspective of long-term utility.

items.abstract: Vision Foundation Models (VFMs) are widely used in computational pathology but remain sensitive to domain shifts arising from variations in staining, tissue preparation, and scanner hardware. items.abstract: We study risk-averse decision making, in which an agent selects actions while being uncertain about the true system state. items.abstract: Social power plays a fundamental role in shaping human interaction, yet computational studies of power remain limited to narrow linguistic and cultural settings. items.abstract: Real-time classification during language model inference is valuable for safety filtering, behavioral analysis, and model monitoring, but current approaches force a trade-off between accuracy and efficiency. items.title: Emergent aggregation from collective foraging
items.abstract: Collective behaviour in living systems is usually modelled as the outcome of a \emph{direct} social drive: agents are rewarded, or hard-wired, to align with or approach their neighbours. Here we show that aggregation can instead emerge from an \emph{indirect} objective. We let reinforcement learning foragers, initially performing a random walk, optimize their dynamics from a purely individual reward for finding replenishable targets, while perceiving only their conspecifics and never the targets themselves. As the visual range grows, the agents undergo a sharp crossover from an environment-tuned individual search to a scale-agnostic collective one, and this crossover coincides with the onset of spatial aggregation. Thus a collective phase arises as a by-product of optimal foraging, without any direct reward for grouping. A minimal analytical first-passage model reproduces the transition as a crossover between the two search strategies. Our results identify indirect, resource-driven reward as a generic route to emergent collective phenomena.

items.abstract: Large language model (LLM) inference serving is priced by tokens, but GPU energy is consumed over inference windows. This accounting mismatch makes token-normalized metrics incomplete, since average output-token energy can decrease even when total request energy increases. We characterize this behavior with a decomposed energy model: a fixed one-time prefill with a fixed generation setup cost, while each output-token generation step adds marginal step energy. items.abstract: Text simplification aims to make complex texts easier to understand while preserving their original meaning. Recent large language models can perform simplification through prompting, but it remains unclear whether adding explicit linguistic information about sentence complexity to the prompt improves their outputs. We investigate this question for multilingual sentence-level Easy-to-Read simplification in Catalan, Spanish, and Italian. Using Qwen3-8B, we compare a baseline prompt, a gold-cue prompt enriched with gold linguistic cues, and a predicted-cue prompt enriched with automatically predicted cues. Predicted-cue prompting obtains the best overall scores across all four metrics, although the gains over the baseline are small. items.title: String: An Agentic OS Where Every App Is a Markdown File
items.abstract: LLM agents have become a new class of software user, but every surface they work through was designed for someone else. items.abstract: Knowledge-intensive reasoning requires Large Language Models (LLMs) to ground answers in provided evidence. items.abstract: Multi-Agent Systems (MAS) have recently moved from static workflows toward dynamically generated collaboration topologies. items.abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) has recently emerged as a popular post-training paradigm for large language models (LLMs), providing an efficient way to transfer the knowledge and capabilities of teacher models into student models. items.abstract: Post-deployment changes to large language models can alter behavior while leaving routine outputs largely unchanged, creating a challenge for AI governance when model weights are proprietary. items.abstract: AI-assisted qualitative data analysis (QDA) offers unprecedented opportunities to streamline software engineering (SE) research, yet uncritical use risks compromising analytical rigor and flooding the field with accelerated production of low-quality research. items.title: PCBnet: A Dataset and Automatic Construction of SPICE Netlists from Schematic Images
items.abstract: Printed circuit boards (PCBs) are fundamental to modern electronic systems, yet AI-driven PCB design automation remains constrained by the lack of large-scale paired schematic-netlist datasets. PCB schematics are particularly challenging due to diverse component types, complex wiring topologies, and noisy textual annotations. To address this gap, we present PCBnet, a large-scale PCB schematic dataset comprising over 300 real-world designs with annotated pins and paired SPICE netlists. It contains more than 50,000 component instances, 150,000 wires, 100,000 text regions, and 400,000 characters. We further develop an automated schematic-to-netlist pipeline that combines visual recognition, topology construction, and domain-knowledge-guided multi-agent correction. The proposed method achieves 94.54% component detection mAP, 98.57% text recognition accuracy, and 84.47% end-to-end connectivity accuracy. PCBnet provides a benchmark and data foundation for future AI-driven PCB design automation.

items.title: AI Alignment through a Game-theoretic Lens: A Survey
items.abstract: As large language models and increasingly capable AI agents are deployed in high-risk settings, aligning them with complex human values has become a central challenge. Existing alignment methods, while effective in improving helpfulness, harmlessness, and controllability, often struggle to capture real-world preferences that are context-dependent, non-transitive, and shaped by dynamic multi-party interactions. This survey reviews AI alignment through a game-theoretic lens. Specifically, it organizes recent progress around key game-theoretic elements and synthesizes the literature along three challenges: preference diversity, alignment priority, and temporal dynamics. This perspective clarifies where current alignment methods genuinely benefit from game-theoretic analysis, where the framework is looser, and what challenges remain in building robust, adaptive, and verifiable AI systems.

items.title: Rubric-to-Code Credit Assignment for Reinforcement Learning
items.abstract: Interactive web application generation requires models to produce usable HTML, CSS, and JavaScript applications from natural language requests. items.title: OpenStamp: A Watermark for Open-Source Language Models
items.abstract: With the growing prevalence of large language model (LLM) generated content, watermarking is considered a promising approach for attributing text to LLMs and distinguishing it from human-written content. items.title: There and Back Again: Bidirectional Diffusion Bridges for Multimodality Translation
items.abstract: Multimodality translation (e.g., text-to-image) is a core generative AI task. items.abstract: We study the properties of the cumulative offer mechanism (COM) when institutions' choice functions satisfy strong observable substitutability (strong OS). Second, we show that when choice functions are strongly OS, weak group strategy-proofness of the COM reduces to individual strategy-proofness. However, strong OS is neither necessary nor "almost necessary" for this reduction.

_analysis.summary: This paper analyzes the cumulative offer mechanism (COM), a method for matching institutions (like platforms or regulators) with participants (like users or advertisers), when the choice functions of these institutions satisfy 'strong observable substitutability' (strong OS). It shows that strong OS can be characterized by properties like IR monotonicity and weak Maskin monotonicity, and that weak group strategy-proofness of the COM simplifies to individual strategy-proofness under strong OS. 'Strong OS' is a technical condition meaning choices are predictable and substitutable, while 'COM' is a mechanism for fair allocation.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: While the paper focuses on abstract matching mechanisms, its insights into strategy-proofness and substitutability could indirectly inform platform design or regulatory tools in digital markets.
_analysis.market_signal: Signals growing academic interest in designing robust, strategy-proof mechanisms for digital platforms, which may influence future regulatory approaches to platform fairness.

items.title: Do Customer Disclosures Affect Suppliers' Internal Capital Allocation Decisions?
items.abstract: This study examines whether customer disclosures affect how supplier firms allocate capital across business segments. Customer disclosures can shape supplier investment decisions through two competing channels. They can improve suppliers' information about downstream demand, helping suppliers align capital with growth opportunities ("information channel"), or erode incumbent suppliers' private information advantage, inducing costly investments to defend customer relationships ("competitive-threat channel"). I use the adoption of SFAS 131 as a customer-level disclosure shock. Suppliers exposed to expanded customer disclosures experience increased product-market competition and reallocate capital toward segments with relatively weak growth-opportunity signals. Suppliers that deviate from allocations predicted by growth signals are more likely to preserve market share and expand their customer base in subsequent years. Using a novel approach to link supplier segments to customer segments, I show that this reallocation is driven by investing in capacity in affected segments, rather than by a correction of prior under-investment. _analysis.summary: This study examines whether customer disclosures affect how supplier firms allocate capital across business segments. Customer disclosures can shape supplier investment decisions through two competing
_analysis.relevance_explanation: Relates to digital competition policy.

items.title: Sophistication in GenAI Use: Field Evidence from a Large Firm
items.abstract: We study how sophistication in generative AI (genAI) use varies among the back-office workforce of a large firm. Using proprietary data, we observe 713,564 employee prompts and their corresponding large language model responses from nearly 4,000 back-office employees across 15 functional areas over eight months in 2025. We document three main findings. First, senior employees exhibit more sophisticated genAI use, consistent with domain expertise complementing genAI capabilities. Second, sophistication varies considerably across functions and is highest in Strategy, Digital Innovation, and Project Management, three groups that share a focus on firmwide strategic initiatives and organizational change. Third, we observe neither improvements in sophistication over time nor lasting improvements following formal AI training, suggesting that sophisticated use can be difficult to change. Together, our study provides measures of and insights into sophisticated genAI use that managers can use to improve outcomes and that researchers can use in future research.

items.title: Disaffection at Work: Employee Responses to Job-Related Information
items.abstract: Quiet quitting reflects a form of worker disaffection that operates along the intensive margin of labor supply rather than through job exit. We study how alternative workplace narratives shape workers' behavioral responses using a randomized survey experiment on a representative sample of employees in Italy and France. Respondents are exposed to empirically grounded moral framings of work emphasizing either social justice and collective rights or work organization and employment practices. We find that moral framings reallocate behavior across margins: justice-oriented narratives increase detachment while reducing passive disengagement, whereas organization-centered framing generates no systematic effects.

_analysis.summary: This study examines how different moral narratives about work—such as those emphasizing social justice or employment practices—affect employee behavior, including 'quiet quitting' (reducing effort without leaving a job). The research, based on a randomized survey in Italy and France, finds that framing work in terms of justice or collective rights shifts how workers respond, particularly toward disengagement or reduced effort rather than job exit.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: While the paper focuses on workplace behavior, its insights into how moral framings influence labor supply decisions could indirectly inform debates about platform worker power and digital labor markets.
_analysis.market_signal: The study signals that narrative framing can shape labor market dynamics, which may have downstream effects on digital platform ecosystems where gig workers are prevalent.

items.title: Refundable Deposits: How to Restore Cooperation in Finitely Repeated Games
items.abstract: While infinitely repeated games admit a rich set of Nash equilibria, finitely repeated games typically have a much smaller and often inefficient one. We show how to enlarge this set using deposits: in each period a player may place a refundable sum with a neutral intermediary, returned when the game ends and forfeited following a deviation. Paying these deposits is voluntary and incentive compatible at every stage, so no commitment by the players is assumed, the only commitment required being that of the intermediary to a refund rule fixed before play begins. The mechanism sustains payoff profiles more efficient than those of the standard equilibria, without altering the underlying game and without transfers between players. We demonstrate it on the prisoner's dilemma, a congestion game, and a public goods game, all settings where cooperation cannot emerge in the standard finitely repeated version. We also apply it to a dynamic common-pool resource, suggesting that the construction extends beyond repeated stage-games.

_analysis.summary: This paper proposes a mechanism using refundable deposits to encourage cooperation in games that repeat a finite number of times, which typically struggle to sustain efficient outcomes. Players voluntarily place sums with a neutral intermediary, which are refunded at the end of the game unless a player deviates from agreed behavior.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: While the paper focuses on game theory rather than digital markets, its insights on voluntary commitments and intermediaries could inform discussions on enforcing cooperation in digital ecosystems, such as platform governance or algorithmic collusion.
_analysis.market_signal: Signals potential models for incentivizing cooperative behavior in digital markets where repeated interactions are common, such as platform-to-business relationships or AI-driven marketplaces.

items.title: Strategy-Proof and Minimally Wasteful Random Assignment
items.abstract: We study random assignment of indivisible objects among a set of agents with strict preferences and outside options. When agents may rank some objects as unacceptable, we consider different notions of measuring waste of object(s) from an ex-ante perspective. The most natural one is $q$-agent-object-waste whereby both one agent and one of his acceptable objects are unassigned with at least probability $q$. On the one hand, we show that any mechanism satisfying equal treatement of almost equals (whereby any two agents with identical rankings over objects receive the same probability shares for objects they both regard acceptable), strategy-proofness and ex-post weak non-wastefulness (whereby in any assignment in the support we cannot have that both one agent and one of his acceptable objects are unassigned) must be $q$-agent-object-wasteful with $q\geq \frac{1}{6}$. On the other hand, we show that random serial dictatorship (RSD) attains the minimal bound of $\frac{1}{6}$ in this class for four agents or three objects. In addition, we consider $q$-object-wastefulness where an object remains unassigned with probability $q$, while agents, who consider it acceptable, remain unassigned w

_analysis.summary: This paper examines how to fairly and efficiently assign indivisible goods (like job positions or housing) when people have strict preferences and some options are unacceptable to them. It introduces the concept of 'q-agent-object-waste' to measure inefficiency, where both an agent and their acceptable object remain unassigned with at least probability q. The study proves that mechanisms ensuring equal treatment for agents with identical preferences can minimize this waste.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: While the paper focuses on general assignment mechanisms, its insights into fairness and efficiency in resource allocation could indirectly inform discussions on digital platform governance, such as fair access to APIs or data.
_analysis.market_signal: Signals growing academic interest in fairness and efficiency in resource allocation systems, which may influence future digital market regulations like the EU's Digital Markets Act (DMA).

items.title: The Pulse Beneath the Job Title: Monthly Readings of Requirements and Tasks from 750 Million Chinese Job Ads
items.abstract: How do we define an occupation? By its job title? An accountant at a small trading company keeps the books; at a listed firm the same title demands a certified-accountant licence, and the week goes to the reports that regulators and the board read. Same title, different bar, different work. What defines an occupation is who it lets in and what it asks them to do. In a rapidly changing labor market, tracking those requirements and tasks is how to take the market's pulse. Yet no instrument reads both at the speed they change. Official occupational directories like O*NET report one national average per occupation, updated every few years. Job postings are timely but unstructured. Research built on them works from job titles plus proprietary skill keywords, which blur what is asked of a candidate into what a candidate is asked to do. The blur matters, because rising requirements and changing tasks are different events with different causes. We separate them. From 752.6 million job ads posted on China's five leading recruitment platforms between 2022 and 2026, we extract the phrases employers write, unify those that name the same thing, and validate the mapping from text back to entry.

_analysis.summary: This paper argues that occupations should be defined not just by job titles but by the actual requirements (e.g., licenses) and tasks they demand, which vary significantly across firms. It highlights the need for real-time tracking of these changes to understand labor market dynamics, noting that traditional occupational directories like O*NET (the U.S. Department of Labor's occupational database) are too slow to capture rapid shifts.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: While focused on labor markets, the paper’s emphasis on how job requirements and tasks define market access and power could indirectly inform discussions about digital platform labor practices or the competitive dynamics of job-matching platforms.
_analysis.market_signal: The paper signals the importance of granular, real-time data on job requirements to understand evolving labor markets, which could be relevant for platforms like LinkedIn or Indeed in shaping their competitive strategies.

items.title: The Italian Municipality Equitable and Sustainable Well-being Index (MESWI)
items.abstract: This paper develops the Municipal Equitable and Sustainable Well-being Index (MESWI) for all Italian municipalities, extending the 12-domain BES framework to the local level through 49 indicators. Results reveal substantial territorial heterogeneity that regional and provincial statistics may conceal. The North-South divide remains the dominant geographical pattern and is considerably stronger than the difference between inner and non-inner areas. At the same time, municipalities within the same regions and territorial categories display markedly different well-being profiles. Remoteness is associated with weaker services and socio-economic opportunities but also with stronger environmental performance. The MESWI provides a fine-grained picture of multidimensional well-being and a potential information base for the programming, monitoring and evaluation of place-based policies.

_analysis.summary: This paper introduces the Municipal Equitable and Sustainable Well-being Index (MESWI), a tool that measures well-being across 49 indicators for Italian municipalities, revealing stark regional disparities—particularly the long-standing North-South divide in Italy. The study finds that even within the same regions, municipalities can have vastly different well-being profiles, challenging broader regional averages.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: While the paper focuses on socio-economic well-being rather than digital markets, its methodology for measuring local disparities could inform discussions on digital divide and access to digital services, which are relevant to competition policy in digital markets.
_analysis.market_signal: The paper highlights the importance of granular, local-level data in understanding disparities, which may indirectly influence how regulators assess digital market access and competition in underserved regions.

items.title: Simultaneous Envy and Equitability Guarantees
items.abstract: Recent work in fair division has focused on either simultaneously satisfying closely related fairness notions or achieving a single notion across the ex-ante and ex-post worlds. We study the compatibility of two fundamentally different fairness notions: envy-freeness and equitability. For indivisible goods-only and chores-only settings, we study the existence and complexity of simultaneously satisfying their relaxations, revealing sharp contrasts between the two settings. We show that EF1+EQ1 may fail to exist even for normalized, additive valuations. Our main algorithmic result computes an EF1+EQ1 allocation for normalized binary goods with at most seven agents. In sharp contrast, binary chores admit the stronger EFX+EQX guarantee for any number of agents, even without normalization. We further initiate the study of cross-notion ex-ante--ex-post guarantees, asking whether randomized allocations can provide ex-ante guarantees for one notion while preserving ex-post guarantees for another.

items.title: An Anonymized Urn-Based Experimental Dataset on Decision-Making under Risk and Ambiguity
items.abstract: This data paper describes an anonymized release derived from controlled behavioral experiments on decision-making under risk (known probabilities) and ambiguous uncertainty (partially specified or unknown probabilities) in Ellsberg-type urn tasks. The release contains 4,486 decision records from 246 adult participant records across two implementations (laboratory and online). In each task, participants reported their maximum stake to enter a subsequent lottery; these stake responses can be interpreted as proxies for willingness to pay within the implemented incentive mechanism. In a subset of tasks, participants also selected the color they wished to bet on. The online implementation additionally includes ex-post evaluations of perceived uncertainty across situations. The repository further provides detailed game definitions, realized lottery outcomes, participant instructions, and a data dictionary of variables. The source export contained 4,544 decision records; 58 records belonging to five participants younger than 18 were excluded from this release because documentation of guardian permission for unrestricted public data publication was not available. The dataset supports repli

_analysis.summary: This paper presents anonymized experimental data on how people make decisions when facing known risks (like a lottery with clear odds) and unknown risks (where probabilities are unclear or hidden). The study involved 246 adults completing tasks where they decided how much they’d pay to enter a lottery, revealing their risk tolerance. The dataset includes 4,486 decision records from both lab and online settings.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: While the study focuses on behavioral economics, its findings on risk aversion and willingness to pay could indirectly inform how digital platforms design pricing or monetization strategies, but it does not directly address competition policy.
_analysis.market_signal: The methodology could inspire new ways to measure consumer behavior in digital markets, particularly for platforms using opaque pricing or probabilistic incentives.

items.title: The Dynamic Trade-Off of Dual-Class Shares
items.abstract: Dual-class shares allocate control to founders whose firm-specific investments drive firm value but separate control from ownership, raising agency costs. We analyze this trade-off dynamically. Using new data on US dual-class firms spanning 52 years and difference-in-differences designs, we show that valuations rise following dual-class recapitalizations but decline over time, whereas innovative output increases persistently. These effects are concentrated in industries with greater firm-specific investments. We find corresponding results for stock unifications. Investment by mature dual-class firms is less sensitive to opportunities and voting premia increase with maturity. Our results support dynamic treatment effects and yield new policy implications.

_analysis.summary: This study examines the trade-offs of dual-class shares, where founders retain control despite selling shares to outside investors. It finds that dual-class structures initially boost firm valuations and innovation, but these benefits fade over time, especially in industries where founders' specialized knowledge drives success. The paper also analyzes stock unifications (reverting to single-class shares) with similar long-term declines in value.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: While dual-class shares are common in tech firms (e.g., Meta, Alphabet), this paper focuses on firm-level governance rather than digital market competition or platform power.
_analysis.market_signal: Signals that governance structures in tech firms may influence innovation and valuation, but not directly shaping digital market competition dynamics.

items.title: Potentials and Weak Potentials in Acyclic and Weakly Acyclic Games
items.abstract: In a number of large, important families of finite games, not only is the set of pure-strategy Nash equilibria nonempty but it is also reachable from any initial strategy profile by some sequence of myopic single-player moves to a better or best-reply strategy. This weak acyclicity property is weaker than acyclicity of the game, which requires every such sequence to reach an equilibrium. For example, all perfect-information extensive-form games are weakly acyclic, but they are generally not acyclic as even sequences of best-improvement steps may cycle. Weak acyclicity is equivalent to acyclicity of some priority rule, which is a rule that allows only some improvement moves. It is also equivalent to the existence of a weak potential, which unlike a potential increases along some rather than every sequence as above.

_analysis.summary: This academic paper discusses 'weak acyclicity' in game theory, a property where games (including digital markets modeled as games) have at least one stable outcome (Nash equilibrium) reachable from any starting point through gradual improvements by players. It contrasts this with 'acyclicity,' where all such improvement paths must end at an equilibrium. For example, games with perfect information (like some digital market interactions) are weakly acyclic but not necessarily acyclic, as players' moves can cycle without reaching stability.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: While not directly about digital competition, the paper's framework of weakly acyclic games can model digital markets where firms iteratively adjust strategies (e.g., pricing, product features) without guaranteed convergence to equilibrium, highlighting dynamic competitive pressures.
_analysis.market_signal: Signals that digital markets may exhibit unstable or cyclical competitive dynamics due to iterative strategic interactions, complicating predictions of market outcomes.

items.title: Agnostic Sequential Rationality
items.abstract: Agnostic sequential equilibrium (ASE) is a refinement of sequential equilibrium that does not force on the players a single, arbitrary belief system. In addition, whereas sequential equilibrium assumes the players' beliefs to be fully consistent (a notion that is based on perturbations of strategies), ASE employs a novel, simpler and local concept of strong consistency between strategy profiles and off-equilibrium beliefs, which is applicable to a large class of dynamic games, including games with a continuum of actions. In the last respect, the new solution concept is similar to perfect Bayesian equilibrium. It is shown that a strategy profile in an imperfect-information extensive-form game with perfect recall is an ASE precisely when it is a sequential equilibrium with every fully consistent belief system. ASE is generalized by the set-valued solution concept of agnostic sequential polyequilibrium, which allows leaving the players' actions in some information sets partially or completely unspecified.

_analysis.summary: This paper introduces a new game theory concept called *agnostic sequential equilibrium (ASE)*, which refines how players' beliefs are handled in dynamic games without imposing a single, rigid belief system. Unlike traditional models, ASE uses a simpler and more local consistency check between strategies and beliefs, making it applicable to a wide range of games, including those with continuous actions.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: While ASE is a technical advancement in game theory, it does not directly address digital competition policy but could indirectly inform models of strategic behavior in digital markets.
_analysis.market_signal: This paper signals a methodological refinement in modeling strategic interactions, which could influence how economists analyze digital platform dynamics.

items.title: Normative boundaries of AI in scientific work: Evidence from PhD researchers
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly embedded in scientific work, but researchers may not evaluate its use uniformly across research tasks. This study examines task-specific attitudes towards AI among an international, self-selected sample of 3,785 PhD students in STEM and medical and health sciences who participated in Nature's Graduate Survey 2025. We analyse respondents' comfort with using AI for writing a research article, collecting and analysing data, designing experiments, tracking scientific literature, and summarising it. Latent class analysis identifies four distinct attitudinal profiles. The dominant profile reflects a "division of labour," in which AI is widely accepted for literature-related tasks but resisted in activities closely associated with intellectual contribution, such as writing, data analysis, and experimental design. A "status quo" profile is broadly uncomfortable across tasks, an "all-purpose" profile is broadly comfortable, and an "undecided" profile expresses substantial uncertainty. These patterns suggest that attitudes towards AI in research are organised less around a simple acceptance-rejection divide than around task-specific boundaries, li

_analysis.summary: This study surveys 3,785 PhD researchers to understand how comfortable they feel using AI for different scientific tasks, like writing papers or analyzing data. It finds four distinct groups with varying attitudes toward AI, suggesting that AI adoption in research is uneven and task-dependent.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: Reveals how AI tools are being integrated into research workflows, which could influence the demand for and competitive dynamics of AI-powered scientific software and platforms.
_analysis.market_signal: AI adoption in scientific research may accelerate the growth of specialized AI tools, potentially disrupting traditional academic publishing and data analysis markets.

items.title: The Reverse Big Push: Generative AI and Self-Fulfilling Automation
items.abstract: Generative AI relocates the fixed cost of automation. A model provider pays to train a frontier system, while a downstream firm rents capability by usage; the same firm must carry a continuing payroll to supply a human-augmented service. We study this asymmetry in a local service economy with household budgets and a market-clearing wage. Human augmentation earns a larger surplus from an additional customer, whereas automation has the lower break-even scale. Payroll supports demand across sectors. Wage adjustment works against this feedback but does not generally undo it: when the wage-income effect dominates the fall in the wage bill per retained worker, production modes are strategic complements. The economy can then possess both a high-demand human-augmented equilibrium and a low-demand automated equilibrium. The former is the local first best, even when flexible wages prevent a firm-profit ranking. With forward-looking firms and staggered revision opportunities, the same inherited employment structure can support an automation cascade or an augmentation recovery; the anticipated path of later adopters validates the first movers' choices. Under the regularity and boundary conditi

_analysis.summary: This paper examines how generative AI shifts the costs of automation from downstream firms to model providers, creating an asymmetry where AI rental (pay-per-use) competes with human-augmented services. It finds that while human labor generates more surplus per customer, AI has a lower break-even scale, potentially disrupting local service markets. Wage adjustments may not fully counteract these effects.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: It reveals how generative AI's cost structure could reshape market dynamics in digital labor and service industries, threatening incumbents or enabling new entrants.
_analysis.market_signal: Generative AI's pay-per-use model may accelerate automation in service sectors, altering competitive landscapes and labor markets.

items.title: Social Network Structure, Wealth, and Wealth Inequality Across Cultures
items.abstract: Despite theory tying wealth inequality to social structure, empirical evidence has been limited to a few studies based on online social media data. This study uses a very different type of data, expands the global coverage to very different types of societies, and investigates new questions. In particular, we collect data from ~3500 sharing units (households) in 46 communities across the globe, representing considerable human social and cultural diversity. In each, we analyze the relationship between people's material wealth and the structure of social networks: borrowing money, sharing food, working together, socializing, etc. In almost all communities, a sharing unit's material wealth is positively associated with the number of other sharing units it both helps and is helped by. A sharing unit's wealth is also associated with the relative wealth of the sharing units to which it is linked---a form of economic homophily. Notably, communities with greater wealth inequality are also characterized by a network structure in which poorer sharing units are less well connected to wealthier ones. We augment our unique cross-cultural data with other community-level environmental, institutio

_analysis.summary: This study examines how social network structures—specifically borrowing money and sharing food—relate to wealth and wealth inequality across 46 diverse communities worldwide. It challenges prior research that relied on online social media data by using detailed household-level data from ~3,500 sharing units.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: While the study provides insights into social networks and wealth inequality, it does not directly address digital markets or competition policy.
_analysis.market_signal: This research signals the importance of understanding offline social networks in economic behavior, which may indirectly inform platform economics but lacks direct digital market implications.

items.title: Interpersonally Comparable Utility
items.abstract: We develop a theory of measurement scales for utility functions, based on a generalization of the notion of numeraire commodity. Every sufficiently well-behaved utility is denominated in some scale of this form, and conversely, the choice of a compatible scale unit uniquely identifies utilities up to an additive constant. We define a profile of utilities to be interpersonally comparable precisely when they are denominated in a common measurement unit. We study when profiles of comparable utilities exist, as well as how a planner ought to aggregate them, and provide applications to social choice and welfare economics.

_analysis.summary: This paper introduces a new way to measure and compare how different people value things (utility functions) by using a shared 'unit' (like a numeraire commodity) to make their preferences directly comparable. It explores when such comparable measurements are possible and how a planner (like a policymaker) could combine them into a single decision, with applications to social choice theory.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: While this paper focuses on theoretical foundations of utility measurement, its insights could indirectly inform how digital platforms aggregate user preferences or design algorithms, potentially affecting market power dynamics.
_analysis.market_signal: This work signals a deeper methodological foundation for understanding how digital platforms might compare or aggregate user data, which could influence future algorithmic design or regulatory approaches to data portability.

items.title: Theory as data compression
items.abstract: Comparing economic models requires balancing fit against flexibility. Yet standard selection criteria often proxy flexibility using parameter counts, overlooking differences due to functional form and experimental design. This paper introduces a data compression approach for evaluating economic models. Following the Minimum Description Length principle, models are interpreted as codes and evaluated by how effectively they compress data. This perspective yields compression-based analogues of Selten's predictive success and Fudenberg et al.'s completeness and restrictiveness. Unlike Selten's measure, its analogue unifies deterministic and stochastic models in a likelihood framework; unlike Fudenberg et al.'s measures, the proposed framework provides a complete selection criterion. Applications to social preferences, risky choice, and intertemporal choice illustrate the relevance of the approach. In simulations, accounting for flexibility differences due to functional form and experimental design improves model recovery relative to AIC, BIC, and cross-validation. In empirical reanalyses, MDL changes model rankings in favor of more parsimonious specifications.

_analysis.summary: This paper proposes a new way to compare economic models by treating them like data compression tools. Instead of just counting parameters, it evaluates models based on how well they simplify or 'compress' data, using the Minimum Description Length principle. This approach offers fresh criteria for assessing model fit and flexibility, inspired by concepts like Selten's predictive success.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: While the paper introduces a novel methodological framework for economic modeling, it does not directly address digital competition policy or market dynamics.
_analysis.market_signal: This work signals a potential shift in how economic models are evaluated, which could indirectly influence future competition policy analysis.

items.title: Learning Whom to Trust : Decision-Generated Credibility in Social Learning
items.abstract: Social interaction can improve collective learning but also amplify early mistakes. We study this tension when the credibility of social information is generated by the sender's own decision process rather than fixed ex ante. Reinforcement-learning agents make binary choices through a drift--diffusion process that jointly determines choice, decision time, and confidence; decision confidence then becomes social credibility by weighting anticipatory influence and retrospective social learning. Under balanced community exposure, the anticipatory field admits an exact quotient representation. Its local Jacobian is a scalar decision-sensitivity term multiplying the community-coupling matrix, which yields a common-mode amplification threshold and an analytical role for cross-community permeability in damping relative community differences. Monte Carlo experiments show the corresponding non-monotone performance pattern: moderate transmission accelerates correction, whereas strong transmission can lock populations into wrong consensus; low permeability instead sustains disagreement. Ablations reveal a dual role for confidence: credibility-sensitive transmission amplifies social error, whil

_analysis.summary: This paper examines how social learning in digital networks can both improve collective decision-making and amplify early mistakes. It models agents using reinforcement learning to make binary choices, where their decision confidence (generated by their own process) acts as credibility in social interactions. The study finds that under balanced exposure, the system's behavior can be mathematically represented, revealing how credibility dynamics shape collective outcomes.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: This work provides foundational insights into how algorithmic agents generate and propagate credibility in digital ecosystems, which is critical for understanding platform dynamics and potential manipulation risks under the EU's DMA (Digital Markets Act).
_analysis.market_signal: Algorithmic agents' credibility-weighting mechanisms could influence how digital platforms curate and prioritize information, potentially reinforcing market power or enabling new forms of competitive advantage.

items.title: The Paradox of Strategic Altruism
items.abstract: Can altruism serve as the behavioral foundation for efficient institutional design? We study full implementation in Berge equilibrium, the solution concept that formalizes strategic altruism: each agent's opponents collectively maximize her payoff. While Berge equilibrium resolves the Prisoner's Dilemma and can eliminate cooperation failures in social dilemmas, we show that this optimism does not survive the move from individual behavior to institutional design. First, we show that the weak Pareto optimal rule is not implementable in Berge equilibrium. Second, on the unrestricted domain of strict preferences, any social choice rule that is both weakly Pareto efficient and implementable in Berge equilibrium must be dictatorial. Finally, we show that Berge implementability is strictly more demanding than Nash implementability: every social goal achievable under strategic altruism is also achievable under self-interest, but not vice versa. The very feature that makes Berge equilibrium appealing at the behavioral level, that is, opponents protecting each agent's payoff, is precisely what forecloses efficient, non-dictatorial institutions at the design level.

_analysis.summary: This paper explores whether altruism—specifically 'strategic altruism,' where agents' opponents collectively maximize their payoff—can improve institutional design by resolving social dilemmas like the Prisoner’s Dilemma. However, it finds that even this approach fails to implement efficient rules (like the weak Pareto optimal rule) in institutional settings, highlighting limits to cooperative solutions in complex systems.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: While the paper focuses on theoretical institutional design, its insights into cooperative behavior and equilibrium concepts could indirectly inform debates on algorithmic coordination or platform governance in digital markets.
_analysis.market_signal: The study signals that cooperative behavioral models may not easily translate to scalable institutional solutions, cautioning against over-reliance on altruistic assumptions in designing digital market regulations.

items.title: AI worsens climate change, integrated assessment shows
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) interacts with climate in various ways, while a unified analytical framework of this intricate interplay is lacking. To align AI investment with climate policy, we propose such a framework integrating AI's impact on emissions, output, and climate damages into the DICE model. We distinguish between ICT-like and Industrial Revolution (IR)-like AI prospects. Calibrated to the best available evidence, we find that AI development is net polluting. Under current low abatement, ICT-like AI adds 0.1 degree C to 2100 warming, while IR-like AI adds 0.8 degree C. The associated climate costs offset roughly one-fifth and one-quarter of AI's economic gains, respectively. Meeting the 2 degree C target saves the optimal ICT(IR)-like AI investment rate by 2100 from 3.3% (5.1%) under the low-abatement scenario to 3.7% (12.7%), indicating that mitigation is complementary to AI development. We further show that the investment trade-off between AI and abatement is driven primarily by AI's economic prospects, not by its emissions footprint.

_analysis.summary: This academic paper examines how artificial intelligence (AI) impacts climate change by integrating AI's effects on emissions, economic output, and climate damages into the DICE model (a well-known integrated assessment model for climate policy). The study finds that AI development is generally net polluting, with different types of AI (ICT-like vs. Industrial Revolution-like) contributing to varying degrees of global warming by 2100. ICT-like AI could add 0.1°C to 2100 warming, while IR-like AI could add 0.8°C.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: While the paper focuses on AI's environmental impact rather than competition policy, it highlights the energy-intensive nature of AI, which could influence discussions on AI regulation and market power in digital infrastructure.
_analysis.market_signal: The paper signals that AI's energy demands may drive consolidation in cloud computing and data center markets, potentially reinforcing the dominance of large tech firms with the resources to sustain high-energy AI workloads.

items.title: Fair Allocation with Optional Selling
items.abstract: We consider fair allocation of indivisible goods in a setting in which agents have subjective valuation functions over the set of goods, and in addition, goods may be sold at given market prices. In this setting, a fair allocation involves {deciding which goods to sell, how to allocate the unsold goods, and how to divide the money received from the sold goods.} We adapt to this setting the definitions of share-based fairness notions, such as the maximin share (MMS) and the truncated proportional share (TPS), and comparison-based fairness notions such as EF1 and EFX (which we adapt to SEF1 and SEFX). We show the following results when the utility of each agent is additive both over goods and over money. With two agents, there are allocations that are simultaneously MMS and SEFX. With three agents, there are instances in which no allocation gives every agent more than $\frac{11}{12}$-MMS. With any number of agents, there are $\frac{2}{3}$-MMS allocations. There also are allocations that are simultaneously SEFX and $\frac{n}{2n-1}$-TPS. This latter ratio is best possible, even without the SEFX requirement.

_analysis.summary: This paper studies how to fairly divide indivisible goods (like digital assets or platform resources) when some goods can be sold at fixed prices while others are allocated directly. It adapts fairness concepts like the maximin share (MMS) and envy-free up to one good (EF1) to account for optional selling, ensuring balanced outcomes in hybrid economic settings.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: While the paper focuses on theoretical fairness in allocation problems, its insights could indirectly inform discussions on digital market fairness, such as platform resource distribution or data allocation.
_analysis.market_signal: Signals growing academic interest in fairness mechanisms for digital resource allocation, which may influence future platform governance debates.

items.title: Contagious Ambiguity
items.abstract: We study the strategic impact of ambiguity through the channel of higher-order beliefs. We show that even small amounts of prior ambiguity about game payoffs can generate arbitrarily large amounts of higher-order ambiguity. This gives rise to a novel form of contagion: vanishingly small payoff ambiguity can select ``secure'' actions (e.g., non-participation) as the unique equilibrium outcome even when those actions are almost dominated. We highlight two main implications. First, classical robustness results under probabilistic uncertainty break down under ambiguity when players can deviate to secure actions. Second, if a designer can introduce small amounts of payoff ambiguity into a game, this can serve as a powerful tool for unique implementation.

_analysis.summary: This paper examines how uncertainty (called 'ambiguity') in business strategies can spread unpredictably through markets. It finds that even tiny amounts of ambiguity about competitors' actions can lead to extreme caution, causing firms to avoid risky moves like entering a market—even if those moves would normally be profitable. This 'contagion' effect can make markets less competitive by discouraging participation.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: Shows how ambiguity in digital markets (e.g., AI-driven uncertainty) can suppress competitive entry or innovation, reinforcing dominant positions.
_analysis.market_signal: Highlights how strategic uncertainty in tech markets (e.g., AI competition) could lead to defensive behaviors that entrench gatekeepers.

items.title: Dynamics of the Currency Composition of Central Bank Reserves
items.abstract: We examine how macroeconomic and geopolitical developments in the United States, the euro area, and China affect the currency composition of central banks' foreign exchange reserves. Using an unbalanced panel of reserve shares for 53 countries over 1999-2023, we estimate a constrained system of equations that explicitly imposes the adding-up restriction on reserve shares. The results indicate substantial persistence in reserve holdings and significant cross-currency dependence, supporting a system-wide dynamics of reserve composition. In the country fixed-effects specification (1) issuer economic size, (2) uncertainty, (3) sanctions, (4) trade linkages, and (5) issuer credibility are significantly associated with reserve allocation across currencies. With the inclusion of year fixed effects, the persistence and cross-currency dependence remain, while trade linkages and sanctions emerge as the most important determinants of reserve composition. The results highlight the importance of accounting for the compositional nature and interdependence of reserve shares when examining the determinants of global reserve holdings.

_analysis.summary: This academic paper studies how economic and political developments in the U.S., Europe, and China influence which currencies central banks hold as foreign exchange reserves. Using data from 53 countries over 24 years, it finds that reserve currency choices are slow to change and closely linked across different currencies, suggesting a system-wide pattern in how reserves are managed.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: While the paper focuses on central bank reserve currencies rather than digital markets, it provides methodological insights into how macroeconomic and geopolitical factors shape market structure, which can indirectly inform digital competition policy.
_analysis.market_signal: The paper signals that systemic dependencies in financial markets (like reserve currency holdings) may also exist in digital platform ecosystems, where geopolitical and economic shifts could similarly reshape competitive dynamics.

items.title: Participation, selection and indicative bidding in auctions with costly entry
items.abstract: We study auctions with costly entry in which bidders have incomplete information about their affiliated private valuations prior to entry. We examine whether indicative bidding--a mechanism requiring non-binding preliminary bids before entry--can stimulate participation and improve entrant selection, and we compare its performance with unrestricted and capped entry in a controlled laboratory experiment. When entry costs are high, indicative bidding generates significantly more revenue, primarily by increasing participation beyond theoretical predictions. When entry costs are low, its predicted revenue advantage is attenuated by higher-than-predicted selection inefficiency.

_analysis.summary: This academic paper examines how 'indicative bidding'—a system where bidders submit non-binding preliminary offers before committing to enter an auction—can boost participation and improve selection of entrants in auctions with costly entry. In controlled lab experiments, it found that when entry costs are high, indicative bidding increases revenue by encouraging more participation than predicted by theory. When entry costs are low, its effects are less clear.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: While not directly about digital markets, the paper’s insights into auction design and entry costs are relevant to platform economics and the economics of digital advertising auctions, which often rely on similar mechanisms.
_analysis.market_signal: The paper signals that auction design tweaks (like indicative bidding) could influence participation in digital ad markets or platform-mediated transactions, potentially affecting market concentration.

items.title: A Case for Competition in Information Provision
items.abstract: We study how competition among biased news sources affects information and welfare when sources can misrepresent facts at a cost. Monopolistic and competitive market structures admit many equilibria. We develop a common belief-based selection criterion that applies to both and makes welfare comparisons possible. Under the refined outcomes, adding an oppositely biased source improves the receiver's welfare when that source faces sufficiently high misreporting costs. Competition disciplines the incumbent while introducing a few distortions of its own. Better information need not increase total welfare, and distorted advice from a monopolist can raise total welfare. Competition may improve decision-making without being socially beneficial.

_analysis.summary: This paper examines how competition between biased news sources (e.g., media outlets with political leanings) affects the quality of information and overall welfare when sources can distort facts at a cost. It finds that adding a competing source with opposing bias can improve welfare if the new source faces high costs to misreport information, as competition pressures the incumbent to be more truthful, though it may also introduce new distortions.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: The paper provides theoretical insights into how competition in digital information markets (e.g., social media, news aggregators) can discipline dominant platforms or biased providers, which is central to digital competition policy debates.
_analysis.market_signal: The analysis suggests that introducing competing information sources (e.g., alternative platforms or regulatory mandates for diverse viewpoints) could mitigate misinformation and reduce market power in digital information ecosystems.

items.title: Rating Manipulation: Credibility Inversion and Audit Leakage
items.abstract: Online ratings turn a long review history into one public number. This makes sellers easier to compare, but it also gives them a single clear target to manipulate. We study a low-quality seller who can add fake reviews carrying different scores, buyers who infer quality from the displayed average, and a platform that can target particular scores for enforcement. The model separates the rating buyers see from the hidden mix of reviews used to produce it, and the two need not move together. An almost-perfect rating can be less credible than a slightly lower one when low-quality sellers are especially likely to manufacture the top of the scale, so a seller whose buyers become more valuable may display less and sell more. At a fixed displayed rating, targeted enforcement can redirect fake reviews toward other scores rather than eliminate manipulation; buyers do not see this substitution because the displayed average is unchanged. Raw ratings therefore provide only a partial picture of credibility and enforcement, and buyer-oriented ranking should account for what a rating conveys, not only its numerical level.

_analysis.summary: This paper examines how online rating systems—where a single public score aggregates many reviews—can be manipulated by low-quality sellers using fake reviews. It finds that a near-perfect rating may actually be *less* credible than a slightly lower one because it signals extreme manipulation, while a slightly lower score appears more trustworthy despite still being inflated.
_analysis.relevance_explanation: It reveals how rating manipulation undermines consumer trust and market transparency, which are critical for fair competition in digital platforms like e-commerce, app stores, or review-based services.
_analysis.market_signal: Rating systems' vulnerability to manipulation may force platforms to adopt stricter verification or transparency measures, potentially increasing compliance costs and altering competitive dynamics.

_analysis.relevance_explanation: This enforcement action signals scrutiny of deceptive practices in digital financial platforms, which can distort competition and harm consumers, aligning with broader digital market regulation.
_analysis.market_signal: The case signals increased regulatory focus on transparency and fairness in digital financial services, particularly where misleading practices may create unfair advantages for dominant platforms.

synthesis.headline: AI agents, synthetic data and energy costs: three new fronts in digital-market competition
synthesis.executive_summary: Academic work published in late-August 2026 shows how synthetic data, AI agents and energy-aware pricing models are reshaping competitive dynamics in digital markets. Researchers warn that single-process AI-agent architectures create single points of failure that could entrench incumbents [#3], while EU regulators are probing whether AI-powered autobidding in online ads concentrates market power [#40]. Meanwhile, a new benchmark reveals prompt-injection vulnerabilities in long-context LLMs that could trigger regulatory scrutiny [#17]. These developments matter because they map the next battlegrounds for dominance in AI-driven services, cloud infrastructure and digital advertising.

key_themes.theme: AI agents and platform architecture risk
key_themes.description: A formal framework demonstrates that modern AI agents built as single-process plugins share one failure domain, creating systemic reliability risks that could slow innovation and entrench large platforms [#3]. A separate study finds AI agents can bypass tool-use requirements, fabricating data without actually invoking tools, which undermines verification and compliance checks [#15]. These findings matter because they identify structural weaknesses in agentic systems that regulators may target under platform-safety rules.

faq.question: What are the 2-3 most important developments this week?
faq.answer: First, the Polish competition authority (UOKiK) charged the Supergrosz platform with misleading consumers by offering fake credit limits while charging high fees, highlighting risks in digital financial services. Second, research on AI agent vulnerabilities like prompt injection (e.g., CAITLYN and LongPIBench) shows how AI systems can be manipulated, threatening security and trust in AI-driven markets. Third, the rise of culturally adaptive AI (e.g., CultureConverse) may disrupt Western-centric AI dominance by empowering regional players.

faq.question: Which companies or markets are most at risk from regulatory action?
faq.answer: Digital financial platforms like Supergrosz face immediate risk due to UOKiK’s charges for deceptive practices. AI security firms may also face scrutiny if their systems fail to address prompt injection vulnerabilities. Additionally, Western AI incumbents (e.g., Google, Meta) could be challenged by regional players leveraging culturally adaptive AI tools.

faq.question: What should competition lawyers and economists do right now?
faq.answer: Lawyers should monitor UOKiK’s Supergrosz case for precedents on digital financial transparency. Economists should analyze how AI-driven market fragmentation (e.g., plugin marketplaces) affects competition dynamics. Both should track AI security risks (e.g., prompt injection) to advise clients on compliance and liability.

faq.question: What new AI or technology trends could change competition in digital markets?
faq.answer: AI agent marketplaces (e.g., Claude Code plugins) may fragment software tooling, enabling new entrants to compete with incumbents. Culturally adaptive AI (e.g., CultureConverse) could shift global AI power away from Western models. Efficient LLM deployment methods (e.g., TensorRT-LLM) may lower costs for startups, disrupting hardware giants like NVIDIA.

faq.question: What legislation or regulation is being proposed or enforced this week?
faq.answer: Poland’s UOKiK enforced consumer protection laws against Supergrosz for misleading credit limits and high fees. No major new legislation was proposed this week, but ongoing research (e.g., prompt injection defenses) may spur future regulations on AI security standards.

faq.question: What does DMA mean?
faq.answer: DMA stands for the Digital Markets Act, a European Union law that targets large tech companies (e.g., Google, Apple, Meta) with rules to prevent anti-competitive practices like self-preferencing or blocking third-party services. It requires these 'gatekeepers' to allow fair competition, share data, and avoid favoring their own products. The DMA aims to make digital markets more open and contestable for smaller firms. Non-compliance can lead to fines up to 10% of global revenue.
